newsitem.title: GREECE: Blockading Greek farmers ponder next move.
newsitem.headline: Blockading Greek farmers ponder next move.

text.p: Farmers in central Greece returned to their barricades on Friday, facing a tough decision whether to give up a 23-day road blockade after the socialist government again flatly rejected their demands.
The government's unrelenting refusal to make concessions appeared to have weakened farmers in other regions. In Macedonia around Salonika farmers said they were suspending action.
Socialist ministers who met a farmers' committee on Thursday made clear that demands could not be met and farmers returned to their road blocks vowing to stay put.
But the northern farmers who met on Friday decided to give Christmas holidaymakers a break.

"We are suspending our mobilisation due to the holidays," said Nikos Moustakas, a representative of farmers in Macedonia and Thrace. "But if our demands are not met, we will return to the barricades."
Farmers in the central Thessaly region, whose blockade has cut Greece in two and inflicted more than $100 millions of damage on the economy, were meeting on Friday to determine future action.
The government has ruled out using force to remove tractors from roads and restore traffic, and has appealed to opposition parties to help talk the farmers out of continuing the blockades.
"We have responded to (some) demands but the roads remain closed," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters. "I appeal to all who can influence developments to help open the roads."
The government has blamed opposition parties, and especially the small communist party, for inciting the farmers.
Farmers want cheaper fuel, lower taxes and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled as well as more subsidies for weather damages and lost income.
The government says it has secured additional money for damaged crops and that it will consider cheaper fuel but other than that it had no more money to give.
About 7,000 farmers from central Greece travelled to Athens in coaches on Thursday and held a rally outside the parliament to press their demands.
Parliament is debating the 1997 austerity budget, which imposes new taxes and abolishes dozens of tax breaks and has prompted a wave of strikes in recent weeks.
A seamen's strike has also hit transport this week.
On Friday they stopped most ships from docking and clashes erupted when ships tried to leave the ports of Piraeus, near Athens, as well as Patras and Igoumenitsa in western Greece.
Police said the scuffles broke out between truck drivers stranded at ports and seamen stopping them from getting onto ferries.
The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) said it had extended the strike, which began on Monday, to protest against rising unemployment and the abolition of special tax exemptions.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis has stood firm against workers' demands, saying a tight budget was the only way to secure Greece's prospects of joining the European Monetary Union in the next five years.
